summary: Discusses different approaches to configuring networks and identifies a set of requirements for configuration management of IP-based networks.

eli5.summary: It lists what a tool must do to set up lots of network machines correctly.

subtitle: What tools need to do to configure large IP networks automatically

tldr.problem: Manually configuring complex networks with many devices from different vendors is time-consuming and error-prone. Each change must be translated by hand from high-level policies into device-specific commands for every affected router and switch.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3139 identifies 15 requirements for configuration management systems that add a layer of abstraction: administrators specify high-level policies once, and automated translators convert them into device-specific configurations, handling topology and status information automatically.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can manage complexity more efficiently by working at the policy level rather than per-device configuration, though integrating such systems with existing SNMP and MIB infrastructure remains a challenge.

today: RFC 3139 remains the foundational requirements document for network configuration management. While specific technologies like YANG and NETCONF have since been developed to address these requirements, the 15 requirements remain largely applicable to modern configuration management systems, though implementations have evolved to include additional considerations like zero-touch provisioning and cloud-based management.

sections.title: The Configuration Problem
sections.content:
Managing large networks has become increasingly difficult because networks grow in multiple dimensions: more devices, more device types from different vendors, and greater complexity in what devices can do. Traditional configuration management treats each device as an independent box: a network operator creates a model of desired behavior, translates it into low-level commands, and manually pushes those commands to each device.

New technologies like RSVP (for reserved bandwidth) and DiffServ (for quality-of-service differentiation) introduced new requirements. Operators needed to specify policies at the network level (e.g., "provide gold-tier service to these customers") rather than individual device configurations. Existing protocols like SNMP and CLI proved inadequate for this higher-level provisioning. This gap motivated the IETF to define requirements that any configuration management system must satisfy to handle modern IP networks.
sections.eli5: Networks used to be simple: an operator would look at what should happen and write a different set of commands for each device. But now networks have hundreds of devices, and they all need to work together. Someone needed to write down what makes a good configuration system.

sections.title: Moving from Device-Centric to Policy-Based Configuration
sections.content:
Historically, network operators and engineers functioned as configuration translators. They would take high-level policies (like "route voice traffic with low delay"), combine them with network topology information and current status, and manually derive device-local configurations for each router. This model worked when networks were small but became unsustainable at scale.

The RFC proposes a new model with an intermediate layer: high-level policies are first translated into network-wide configuration data (middle-level abstractions representing shared behavior across multiple devices), then automated configuration data translators convert that into device-local configurations for deployment. This approach reduces the device-specific knowledge operators must have and allows automated tools to handle the tedious translation work. The abstraction layer provides flexibility, allowing the translators to consider topology, status information, and device capabilities when generating specific commands.
sections.eli5: Old way: someone smart thinks about every device and writes commands for each one. New way: someone writes down what should happen at the network level, and a computer figures out what each device needs.

sections.title: 15 Essential Requirements for Configuration Management
sections.content:
The RFC identifies 15 requirements that a configuration management system MUST meet. The first five address the core provisioning function: the system must support high-level network-wide configuration abstraction, translate it to device-specific configurations considering device capabilities, interpret device status in context of network policies, provision complete or partial configuration changes (with support for fast switchovers), and allow devices to send feedback about their configuration and status.

Requirements six through ten address operational flexibility and reliability: the system must support dynamic configuration changes triggered by network events, provide efficient mechanisms superior to CLI and SNMP for bulk configuration, include security features (access control, authentication, integrity-checking, replay-protection, and privacy), support configuration expiration times, and provide error detection and recovery. Requirements eleven through fifteen address control, auditability, reliability, and extensibility: the system must prevent misconfiguration from concurrent writes, allow tracing of who changed what and when, support redundancy for both network elements and management platforms, remain flexible and extensible for future evolution, and leverage existing SNMP management knowledge and MIBs.
sections.eli5: The requirements say the system must be able to: say what should happen at a high level; translate that to each device; handle device feedback; support fast changes; be secure; prevent mistakes; log who changed what; handle failures; and grow as needs change.

sections.title: Security and Trust in Configuration Management
sections.content:
Requirement 8 emphasizes that configuration management systems MUST provide security mechanisms because configuration data controls the behavior of network infrastructure. The system must ensure the integrity and authenticity of configuration data at all times, meaning administrators must be able to verify that the configuration they are viewing or modifying has not been tampered with. In cases where configuration contains sensitive information (like access control lists or customer-specific policies), the system MUST support privacy protection both at rest and during transmission or provisioning operations.

Requirement 12 addresses the audit trail: configuration management systems must provide facilities to trace back configuration changes with at least host and user-based authentication granularity. This allows administrators to determine who made which changes and when, supporting both troubleshooting and compliance audits. The requirements note that access control and authentication should be flexible, ideally supporting user-role based access with different privileges for different operators.
sections.eli5: People who change network configuration should be authenticated and what they do should be logged. Configuration data traveling over the network should be encrypted. And you should be able to look back and see who did what and when.
